8.content:
[![Image 1: Engagers](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/17thC_dragoon%27s_helmet.JPG/1100px-17thC_dragoon%27s_helmet.JPG)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#/media/File:17thC_dragoon%27s_helmet.JPG)

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Engagers&action=edit&section=0&oldformat=true)The **Engagers** were a faction of the [Scottish](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Scotland "Scotland") [Covenanters](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Covenanters "Covenanters"), who made "**The Engagement**" with King [Charles I](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") in December 1647 while he was imprisoned in [Carisbrooke Castle](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle") by the [English Parliamentarians](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/English_Parliamentarians "English Parliamentarians") after his defeat in the [First Civil War](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War").

**Quick facts** The Engagers, Founded ...

[![Image 2: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg/640px-The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#/media/File:The_Solemn_League_And_Covenant.jpg)

The [Solemn League and Covenant](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant") agreed by English and Scottish Presbyterians in 1643

In the 17th and 18th centuries, politics and religion were closely linked; it is impossible to understand differences between Engagers, Royalists or [Kirk Party](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") political views without an appreciation of these distinctions.

'[Presbyterian](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity")' versus '[Episcopalian](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Episcopal_polity "Episcopal polity")' implied differences in governance, not [doctrine](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Doctrine "Doctrine"). Episcopalian meant rule by bishops, appointed by the monarch; Presbyterian structures were controlled by [Elders](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Elder_/(Christianity/) "Elder (Christianity)"), nominated by their congregations. Arguments over structure or governance of the church were as much about politics and the power of the monarch as religious practice; political divisions often centred on different interpretations of this.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-1)

The [Protestant Reformation](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/English_Reformation "English Reformation") created a [Church of Scotland](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland"), or 'kirk', Presbyterian in structure and governance, and predominantly [Calvinist](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Calvinism "Calvinism") in doctrine. When [James VI and I](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/James_VI_and_I "James VI and I") became king of England in 1603, a unified Church of Scotland and England governed by bishops became the first step in his vision of a centralised, Unionist state.[\[2\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStephen201055%E2%80%9358-2) Although both churches were nominally Episcopalian, they were very different in doctrine; even bishops in Scotland viewed many [Church of England](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Church_of_England "Church of England") practices as little better than Catholicism.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonald199875%E2%80%9376-3)

[![Image 3: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg/320px-1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#/media/File:1st_Marquess_of_Montrose.jpg)

[James Graham, Marquis of Montrose](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/James_Graham,_1st_Marquis_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose"); Royalist commander in Scotland 1644–1645, but a Covenanter general 1638 to 1640

Efforts by [Charles I](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") to impose uniform practices led to the 1638 [National Covenant](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/National_Covenant "National Covenant"), whose signatories pledged to resist liturgical 'innovations'. In December 1638, bishops were expelled from the kirk; when Charles attempted to use military force, he was defeated in the 1639 and 1640 [Bishops' Wars](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bishops'_Wars "Bishops' Wars"), which left the [Covenanter](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Covenanter "Covenanter") party in control of Scotland.[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackieLenmanParker1986204%E2%80%93205-4)

Calvinists believed a 'well-ordered' monarchy was part of God's plan; as a result, the vast majority of Covenanters agreed monarchy itself was divinely ordered but disagreed on who held ultimate authority in clerical affairs.[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacleod20095%E2%80%9319_passim-5) Royalists and Engagers tended to argue the king held supreme authority, but that did not necessarily mean they supported bishops and individual motives were very complex. Many fought for both Covenant and king at different times, including [Montrose](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/James_Graham,_1st_Marquis_of_Montrose "James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose").[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris201553%E2%80%9354-6)

When the [First English Civil War](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") began in 1642, Scotland initially remained neutral, but became involved in the [Irish Rebellion](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 "Irish Rebellion of 1641"); the bitterness of this conflict radicalised views in Scotland and Ireland.[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005142-7) The Covenanter faction known as the [Kirk Party](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party"), led by [Argyll](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), saw religious union with England as the best way to preserve a Presbyterian kirk and in October 1643 the [Solemn League and Covenant](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Solemn_League_and_Covenant "Solemn League and Covenant") agreed a Presbyterian Union in return for Scottish military support.[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobertson2014125-8)

Royalists and moderates in both Scotland and England opposed union, as did the religious [Independents](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Independent_/(religion/) "Independent (religion)") like [Oliver Cromwell](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell"), who dominated the [New Model Army](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") and opposed any state-ordered church. Both Covenanters and their English allies saw the Independents as a bigger threat than the Royalists and when Charles surrendered in 1646, they began negotiations to restore him to the English throne.[\[9\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005420%C2%B7423-9)

[![Image 4: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg/320px-The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#/media/File:The_Marquess_of_Argyll.jpg)

[Marquess of Argyll](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll"), whose [Kirk Party](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Kirk_Party "Kirk Party") opposed the Engagement

The Scots nominated three Commissioners to negotiate with Charles; [Lauderdale](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/John_Maitland,_1st_Duke_of_Lauderdale "John Maitland, 1st Duke of Lauderdale"), [Lanark](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/William_Hamilton,_2nd_Duke_of_Hamilton "William Hamilton, 2nd Duke of Hamilton") and [Loudoun](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/John_Campbell,_1st_Earl_of_Loudoun "John Campbell, 1st Earl of Loudoun"). In December 1647, Charles agreed to impose Presbyterianism in England for three years and suppress the Independents, but his refusal to take the Covenant himself split the Scots.[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-10) It was not until April 1648 the Engagers achieved a majority in the [Scottish Parliament](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Parliament_of_Scotland "Parliament of Scotland"); Argyll's Kirk Party did not trust Charles, objected to an alliance with English and Scots Royalists, and denounced the Engagement as 'sinful.'[\[11\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMitchisonFryFry2002223%E2%80%93224-11)

Most of the Scottish army had been demobilised and efforts to recruit new regiments were undermined when many refused to serve, including their most experienced generals, [Lord Leven](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Alexander_Leslie,_1st_Earl_of_Leven "Alexander Leslie, 1st Earl of Leven") and [David Leslie](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/David_Leslie_/(Scottish_general/) "David Leslie (Scottish general)"). The inexperienced [Duke of Hamilton](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/James_Hamilton,_1st_Duke_of_Hamilton "James Hamilton, 1st Duke of Hamilton") was given command, with the [Earl of Callendar](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/James_Livingston,_1st_Earl_of_Callendar "James Livingston, 1st Earl of Callendar") as his subordinate. When deputy to Leven, Callendar's overestimation of his military abilities had led to constant conflict and this was repeated with Hamilton. His commander of infantry, [William Baillie](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/William_Baillie_/(soldier/) "William Baillie (soldier)"), had direct experience of the New Model Army and doubted their ability to defeat it.[\[12\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005424-12)

After dispersing Kirk Party dissidents at [Mauchline Muir](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Mauchline_Muir "Battle of Mauchline Muir") in June 1648, a poorly trained Engager army of 9,000 marched into England. The [Second English Civil War](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War") was intended as a series of Royalist risings in England and Wales, with the Scots providing support. By the time Hamilton's army entered [Lancashire](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Lancashire "Lancashire") in early August, the other revolts had been suppressed and Cromwell routed the Engagers at [Preston](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Preston_/(1648/) "Battle of Preston (1648)") on 19 August. Hamilton was taken prisoner and executed in March 1649.[\[13\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005470-13)

Defeat at Preston led to the collapse of the Engager regime; the Kirk Party took control of [Edinburgh](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") and although repulsed at [Stirling](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Stirling_/(1648/) "Battle of Stirling (1648)") in September, a new civil war seemed imminent. However, with Cromwell's support, Argyll took control and expelled his Engager opponents, with English troops being withdrawn.[\[13\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005470-13)

The 1649 [Act of Classes](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Act_of_Classes "Act of Classes") banned Engagers and Royalists from holding political or military office and established the Kirk Party as the government of Scotland. However, the execution of Charles in January 1649 was viewed by Covenanters as an offence against God; they proclaimed his son [Charles II](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") King of Scotland and Great Britain. In the 1650 [Treaty of Breda](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Treaty_of_Breda_/(1650/) "Treaty of Breda (1650)"), they agreed to restore Charles to the English throne; in return he accepted the Covenant. Defeats by Cromwell at [Dunbar](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Dunbar_/(1650/) "Battle of Dunbar (1650)") and [Worcester](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Worcester "Battle of Worcester") resulted in Scotland being incorporated into the [Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Commonwealth_of_England,_Scotland_and_Ireland "Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland") in 1654.[\[14\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Engagers#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2005520-14)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Former Scottish Presbyterian political party (1647-1651)

Not to be confused with [Kirik Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirik_Party "Kirik Party").

| 
Kirk Party



 |
| --- |
| [Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_leader "Party leader") | [The Marquess of Argyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Campbell,_1st_Marquess_of_Argyll "Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquess of Argyll") |
| Founded | 1647 |
| Dissolved | 1651 |
| Split from | [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters") |
| Religion | [Presbyterianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism "Presbyterianism") ([Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland")) |
| 

*   [Politics of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Scotland "Politics of Scotland")
*   [Political parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_Scotland "List of political parties in Scotland")
*   [Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Scotland "Elections in Scotland")



 |

The **Kirk Party** were a radical [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism "Presbyterianism") faction of the [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters "Covenanters") during the [Wars of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Wars of the Three Kingdoms"). They came to the fore after the defeat of the [Engagers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engagers "Engagers") faction in 1648 at the hands of [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") and the [English Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Parliament "English Parliament").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party#cite_note-DS08-1) They purged the Covenanters' General Assembly and army of "ungodly elements"[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party#cite_note-ML92-2) and crowned [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") as King of Scotland in 1651, in return for his explicit endorsement of their religious and political agenda in the [Treaty of Breda (1650)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Breda_/(1650/) "Treaty of Breda (1650)").

[Kirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_/(word/) "Kirk (word)") is a Scottish word meaning a church, or more specifically, the [Church of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scotland "Church of Scotland").

The Kirk party's religious zeal did not help their cause militarily. In the month before the [Battle of Dunbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dunbar_/(1650/) "Battle of Dunbar (1650)") they chose to institute a searching three-day examination of the political and religious sentiments of the Scottish army. The result was that the army was purged of "Malignants", 80 officers and 3000 experienced soldiers, while it lay within musket shot of the enemy.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party#cite_note-ML92-2) Their ranks were to some extent made up with replacements with strong spiritual beliefs but little military experience. The Kirk party were therefore discredited when their army was routed by Cromwell's [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") at the Battle of Dunbar, in September 1650.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party#cite_note-DS08-1)

Thereafter, a more representative faction came to the fore in Scottish politics, which tried to reconcile (at least temporarily) the different factions of the Covenanters and Scottish Royalists to resist Cromwell's invasion of Scotland. However, they in turn were defeated at the [Battle of Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Worcester "Battle of Worcester") in 1651,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Party#cite_note-ML92-2) leading eventually to Scotland's incorporation into the [Commonwealth of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England").

The Kirk party were disparagingly called "whiggamores" or "[whigs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_/(disambiguation/) "Whig (disambiguation)")" by their Scottish opponents (See the [Whiggamore Raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiggamore_Raid "Whiggamore Raid")). The nickname was later applied (equally offensively) to those, headed by Anthony Ashley Cooper, [Earl of Shaftesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Ashley_Cooper,_1st_Earl_of_Shaftesbury "Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury"), calling for the exclusion of [James, Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James,_Duke_of_York "James, Duke of York") from the English throne on the grounds of his Catholicism.

Battle of Preston
-----------------

Type of action: Ground battle in the English Civil War of 1642–1651

**Date:** August 17-19, 1648

**Location:** Preston, Lancashire (twenty-five miles northwest of Manchester)

**Combatants:** 17,600 Royalists vs. 14,000 Parliamentarians

**Principal commanders:**_Royalist_, James Hamilton, third marquess and first duke of Hamilton (1606–1649), Sir Marmaduke Langdale (1598–1662); _Parliamentarian_, Oliver Cromwell (1599–1658)

**Result:** The New Model Army routed the armies of Langdale and Hamilton and effectively ended Royalist resistance

The forces of James Hamilton, third marquess and first duke of Hamilton, who was unaware of the close proximity of the Parliamentary army, were spread between Lancaster and Wigan when [Oliver Cromwell](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/oliver-cromwell) sent a force of 200 horsemen and 400 infantry to probe Sir Marmaduke Langdale’s defenses at Preston on August 17, 1648. The divided and confused Royalist army, ineptly commanded by Hamilton, had not anticipated a fight there and had no strategy to confront the enemy. Cromwell’s advance party came upon a raw company, and his veterans quickly dispersed them. Over the next three days, in cramped, wet terrain, the seasoned New Model Army engaged in a vigorous and bloody battle with Langdale’s forces, supported by the advancing Scots. Cromwell successfully split the English and Scottish armies, defeated them convincingly, and claimed more than 10,000 prisoners by battle’s end. Hamilton surrendered at Uttoxeter, Staffordshire, on August 22, and Langdale retreated north.

Significance
------------

The Battle of Preston concluded the second phase of the [English Civil War](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/english-civil-war-1642-1651) and initiated a chain of events that culminated with the execution of [Charles I](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/charles-i) and the establishment of the Commonwealth.

Bibliography
------------

Baker, Anthony. _A Battlefield Atlas of the English Civil War_. London: Ian Allan, 1986.

Emberton, Wilfrid. _The English Civil War, Day by Day_. Phoenix Mill, Gloucestershire, England: Alan Sutton, 1995.

Gentles, Ian. _The New Model Army in England, Ireland, and Scotland, 1645–1653_. Oxford: Blackwell, 1992.

Woolrych, Austin. _Battles of the English Civil War: Marston Moor, Naseby, Preston_. New York: Macmillan, 1961. Reprint. London: Pimlico, 1991.

| [Patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patron_saint "Patron saint") | [Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampshire "Hampshire"); [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester "Winchester"); [Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark "Southwark"); the [weather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather "Weather") |

**Swithun** (or **Swithin**; [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English_language "Old English language"): _Swīþhūn_; [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _Swithunus_; died 2 July 863) was an Anglo-Saxon [bishop of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Winchester "Bishop of Winchester") and subsequently patron saint of [Winchester Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_Cathedral "Winchester Cathedral"). His historical importance as bishop is overshadowed by his reputation for posthumous miracle-working.

Swithun was [Bishop of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Winchester "Bishop of Winchester") from his consecration on 30 October 852 until his death on 2 July 863.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-1) However, he is scarcely mentioned in any document of his own time. His death is entered in the Canterbury manuscript of the _[Anglo-Saxon Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_Chronicle "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle")_ (MS F) under the year 861.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-2) He is recorded as a witness to nine charters, the earliest of which (S 308) is dated 854.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-3)

More than a hundred years later, when [Dunstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunstan "Dunstan") and [Æthelwold of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelwold_of_Winchester "Æthelwold of Winchester") were inaugurating their church reform, Swithun was adopted as patron of the restored church at Winchester, formerly dedicated to [St Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Peter "St Peter") and [St Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_of_Tarsus "Paul of Tarsus"). His body was transferred from its almost forgotten grave to Æthelwold's new basilica on 15 July 971; according to contemporary writers, numerous miracles preceded and followed the move.

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/St-Swithin.jpg/250px-St-Swithin.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St-Swithin.jpg)

Swithun shown in the [Benedictional of St Æthelwold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedictional_of_St_%C3%86thelwold "Benedictional of St Æthelwold"), [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester "Winchester"), 10th century. [British Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Library "British Library"), London

The revival of Swithun's fame gave rise to a mass of legendary literature. The so-called _Vita S. Swithuni_ of [Lantfred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lantfred "Lantfred") and [Wulfstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wulfstan_the_Cantor "Wulfstan the Cantor"), written about 1000, hardly contains any biographical fact; all that has in later years passed for authentic detail of Swithun's life is extracted from a late eleventh-century [hagiography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagiography "Hagiography") ascribed to [Goscelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goscelin "Goscelin") of St Bertin's, a monk who came over to England with [Hermann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_/(bishop_of_Salisbury/) "Herman (bishop of Salisbury)"), [bishop of Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Salisbury "Bishop of Salisbury") from 1058 to 1078. According to this writer Saint Swithun was born in the reign of [Egbert of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egbert_of_Wessex "Egbert of Wessex"), and was ordained priest by [Helmstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmstan "Helmstan"), bishop of Winchester (838-c. 852). His fame reached the king's ears, and he appointed him tutor of his son, [Æthelwulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelwulf_of_Wessex "Æthelwulf of Wessex") (alias Adulphus), and considered him one of his chief friends.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-webster-4) However, [Michael Lapidge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Lapidge "Michael Lapidge") describes the work as "pure fiction" and shows that the attribution to Goscelin is false.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-5)

Under Æthelwulf, Swithun was appointed bishop of Winchester, to which [see](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_see "Episcopal see") he was consecrated by Archbishop [Ceolnoth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceolnoth "Ceolnoth"). In his new office he was known for his piety and his zeal in building new churches or restoring old ones. At his request Æthelwulf gave the tenth of his royal lands to the Church. Swithun made his diocesan journeys on foot; when he gave a banquet he invited the poor and not the rich. [William of Malmesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_of_Malmesbury "William of Malmesbury") adds that, if Bishop [Ealhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eahlstan "Eahlstan") of [Sherborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherborne "Sherborne") was Æthelwulf's minister for temporal matters, Swithun was the minister for spiritual matters.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-webster-4)

Swithun's best-known miracle was his restoration on a bridge of a basket of eggs that workmen had maliciously broken. Of stories connected with Swithun the two most famous are those of the Winchester egg-woman and Queen Emma's ordeal. The former is to be found in the hagiography attributed to Goscelin, the latter in [Thomas Rudborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Rudborne "Thomas Rudborne")'s _Historia major_ (15th century), a work which is also responsible for the story that Swithun accompanied [Alfred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_the_Great "Alfred the Great") on his visit to [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") in the 850s. He died on 2 July 862. On his deathbed Swithun begged that he should be buried outside the north wall of his cathedral where passers-by should pass over his grave and raindrops from the eaves drop upon it.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-webster-4)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Wincath1-11S7-9724wiki.jpg/330px-Wincath1-11S7-9724wiki.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wincath1-11S7-9724wiki.jpg)

St Swithun's memorial shrine in the [retrochoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retroquire "Retroquire") of [Winchester Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_Cathedral "Winchester Cathedral") in [Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampshire "Hampshire"), where the saint's relics were originally kept

Swithun's [feast day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feast_day "Feast day") in England is on 15 July and in Norway (and formerly in medieval Wales) on 2 July. He is also listed on 2 July in the [Roman Martyrology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Martyrology "Roman Martyrology"). He was moved from his grave to an indoor [shrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrine "Shrine") in the [Old Minster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Minster,_Winchester "Old Minster, Winchester") at [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester "Winchester") in 971. His body was probably later split between a number of smaller shrines. His head was certainly detached and, in the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), taken to [Canterbury Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_Cathedral "Canterbury Cathedral"). [Peterborough Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peterborough_Cathedral "Peterborough Cathedral") had an arm.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-6) His main shrine was transferred into the new [Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_architecture "Norman architecture") cathedral at [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester "Winchester") in 1093. He was installed on a 'feretory platform' above and behind the high altar. The [retrochoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrochoir "Retrochoir") was built in the early 13th century to accommodate the huge numbers of pilgrims wishing to visit his shrine and enter the 'holy hole' beneath him. His empty [tomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb "Tomb") in the ruins of the Old Minster was also popular with visitors. The shrine was only moved into the retrochoir itself in 1476. It was [demolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demolition "Demolition") in 1538 during the [English Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation"). A modern representation of it now stands on the site.

The shrine of Swithun at Winchester was supposedly a site of numerous miracles in the Middle Ages. [Æthelwold of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelwold_of_Winchester "Æthelwold of Winchester") ordered that all monks were to stop whatever they were doing and head to the church to praise God every time that a miracle happened. A story exists that the monks at some point got so fed up with this, because they sometimes had to wake up and go to the church three or four times each night, that they decided to stop going. St Swithun then appeared in a dream to someone (possibly two people) and warned them that if they stopped going to the church, then miracles would cease. This person (or persons) then warned the monks about the dream they had, and the monks then caved in and decided to go to the church each time a miracle happened again.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-7)

Swithun is [remembered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendar_of_saints_/(Church_of_England/) "Calendar of saints (Church of England)") in the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") with a [Lesser Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesser_Festival_/(Anglicanism/) "Lesser Festival (Anglicanism)") on [15 July](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_15 "July 15").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-8)

Swithun is regarded as one of the saints to whom one should pray in the event of drought.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-farmers-9)

There are in excess of forty [churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_/(building/) "Church (building)") dedicated to St Swithun, which can be found throughout the south of England, especially in [Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampshire "Hampshire") – see [this list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Swithun%27s_Church_/(disambiguation/) "St Swithun's Church (disambiguation)"). An example is [St Swithun's, Headbourne Worthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Swithun%27s_Church,_Headbourne_Worthy "St Swithun's Church, Headbourne Worthy"), to the north of Winchester. This church is surrounded on three sides by a brook that flows from a spring in the village; the [lych gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lych_gate "Lych gate") on the south side is also a bridge over the brook, which is unusual. Other churches dedicated to St Swithun can be found at [Walcot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walcot,_Bath "Walcot, Bath"),[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-walcot-10) [Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Swithin%27s_Church,_Lincoln "St Swithin's Church, Lincoln"), [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Swithun%27s_Church,_Worcester "St Swithun's Church, Worcester"),[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-worcester-11) Cheswardine, Shropshire and western [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"), where [Stavanger Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stavanger_Cathedral "Stavanger Cathedral") is dedicated to him. He is also commemorated at St Swithin's Lane in the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London") (site of the former church of [St Swithin, London Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Swithin,_London_Stone "St Swithin, London Stone"), demolished after wartime damage in 1962), [St Swithun's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Swithun%27s_School,_Winchester "St Swithun's School, Winchester") for girls in Winchester and St Swithun's quadrangle in [Magdalen College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalen_College,_Oxford "Magdalen College, Oxford"). In [Stavanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stavanger "Stavanger"), Norway, several schools and institutions are named "St. Svithun" after him.

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/St_Swithun_Statue.jpg/250px-St_Swithun_Statue.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Swithun_Statue.jpg)

Statue of St Swithun originally on the [façade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fa%C3%A7ade "Façade") of [Winchester Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_Cathedral "Winchester Cathedral"); now housed in the [crypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crypt "Crypt")

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Winchester_City_St_Swithun%27s_Bridge.jpg/250px-Winchester_City_St_Swithun%27s_Bridge.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Winchester_City_St_Swithun%27s_Bridge.jpg)

The proverb is sometimes attributed specifically to City Bridge in Winchester, also known as Swithun's Bridge or Soke Bridge[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-12)

The name of Swithun is best known today for a [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") [weather lore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_lore "Weather lore") [proverb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proverb "Proverb"), which says that if it rains on St Swithun's day, 15 July, it will rain for forty days.

> St Swithun's day if thou dost rain  
> For forty days it will remain  
> St Swithun's day if thou be fair  
> For forty days 'twill rain nae mare

A Buckinghamshire variation has:

> If on St Swithun's day it really pours  
> You're better off to stay indoors

Swithun was initially buried outdoors, rather than in his cathedral, apparently at his own request. William of Malmesbury recorded that the bishop left instructions that his body should be buried outside the church, _ubi et pedibus praetereuntium et stillicidiis ex alto rorantibus esset obnoxius_ \[where it might be subject to the feet of passers-by and to the raindrops pouring from on high\], which has been taken as indicating that the legend was already well known in the 12th century.

In 971 it was decided to move his body to a new indoor shrine, and one theory traces the origin of the legend to a heavy shower by which, on the day of the move, the saint marked his displeasure towards those who were removing his remains. This story, however, cannot be traced further back than the 17th or 18th century. Also, it is at variance with the 10th century writers, who all agreed that the move took place in accordance with the saint's desire expressed in a vision. [James Raine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Raine_/(antiquary/) "James Raine (antiquary)") suggested that the legend was derived from the tremendous downpour of rain that occurred, according to the [Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_England "Durham, England") chroniclers, on St.Swithun's Day, 1315.

[John Earle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Earle_/(professor/) "John Earle (professor)") suggests that the legend comes from a [pagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paganism "Paganism") or possibly prehistoric day of [augury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augury "Augury"). In [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [St Medard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medardus "Medardus") (8 June), [Urban of Langres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_of_Langres "Urban of Langres"), and [St Gervase and St Protais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gervasius_and_Protasius "Gervasius and Protasius") (19 June) are credited with an influence on the weather almost identical with that attributed to St Swithun in England. In [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders"), there is [St Godelieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godelieve "Godelieve") (6 July) and in Germany the [Seven Sleepers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Sleepers "Seven Sleepers")' Day (27 June). In Russia it is the day of [Sampson the Hospitable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampson_the_Hospitable "Sampson the Hospitable") (27 June [old style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_style "Old style")).[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-13)

There is a scientific basis to the weather pattern behind the legend of St Swithun's day. Around the middle of July, the [jet stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream "Jet stream") settles into a pattern which, in the majority of years, holds reasonably steady until the end of August. When the jet stream lies north of the [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles "British Isles") then continental high pressure is able to move in; when it lies across or south of the British Isles, Arctic air and Atlantic weather systems predominate.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-14) The most false that the prediction has been, according to the [Guinness Book of Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_Book_of_Records "Guinness Book of Records"), was in 1924 when 13.5 hours of sunshine in London were followed by 30 of the next 40 days being wet, and in 1913 when a 15-hour rainstorm was followed by 30 dry days out of 40.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swithun#cite_note-15)

Top Questions

### 

What happens if it rains on St. Swithin’s Day?

In folklore, St. Swithin’s Day is believed to dictate the weather for the following 40 days. If it rains on this day, it will rain for 40 days; if it is fair, 40 days of fair weather will follow.

### 

What is the St. Swithin’s Day rhyme?

The St. Swithin’s Day rhyme is:

St. Swithin’s day if thou dost rain For forty days it will remain St. Swithin’s day if thou be fair For forty days ’twill rain nae mair.

### 

What is St. Swithin the patron saint of?

St. Swithin is the patron saint of [Winchester Cathedral](https://www.britannica.com/place/Winchester-Cathedral).

### 

Was St. Swithin’s Day mentioned in _The Simpsons_?

St. Swithin’s Day was referenced in the sixth season (1994–95) of the TV show [_The Simpsons_](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-Simpsons). In the first episode, Bart writes a play that mentions the holiday.

**St. Swithin’s Day**, (July 15), a day on which, according to [folklore](https://www.britannica.com/topic/folklore-academic-discipline), the weather for a [subsequent](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/subsequent) period is dictated. In popular belief, if it [rains](https://www.britannica.com/science/rain) on St. Swithin’s Day, it will rain for 40 days, but if it is fair, 40 days of fair [weather](https://www.britannica.com/science/weather) will follow. [St. Swithin](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Swithun) was bishop of Winchester from 852 to 862. At his request he was buried in the churchyard, where rain and the steps of passersby might fall on his grave. According to [legend](https://www.britannica.com/art/legend-literature), after his body was moved inside the cathedral on July 15, 971, a great storm ensued. The first textual evidence for the weather prophecy appears to have come from a 13th- or 14th-century entry in a manuscript at Emmanuel College, Cambridge.

Weather frequently changes around midsummer, and, thus, the tradition that this day influences the weather may stem from earlier, possibly pre-Christian, belief. On the European continent similar beliefs are attached to other saints (e.g., [St. Médard](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Medard-of-Noyon), June 8, France).

This engagement marked the decisive close to the [Second English Civil War](https://sevenswords.uk/english-civil-war-every-battle/). [Oliver Cromwell’s](https://sevenswords.uk/oliver-cromwell/) New Model Army faced a combined Royalist force, largely Scottish Engagers, in a pursuit that turned into a rout and sealed the fate of the militarised uprising.

### Background

[Charles I](https://sevenswords.uk/charles-i-of-england/) had sought to regain his throne by negotiating with a faction of Scots, known as the Engagers, who agreed to assist him in return for ecclesiastical concessions. In response, Cromwell marched north and met Hamilton’s army around Preston.

According to contemporary accounts, “\[in\] one skirmish the commander of their advance guard was killed,” underlining the fierce resistance Cromwell faced even in pursuit.

* * *

Forces
------

### Leaders

**Parliamentarians (New Model Army / Northern Association / Lancashire Militia)**

*   Oliver Cromwell commanded the main New Model Army.
*   John Lambert led Northern Association forces.
*   Regional militia under various local commanders.

**Royalists (Scottish Engagers with English Royalist support)**

*   Duke of Hamilton led the main Scottish Engager army.
*   General William Baillie oversaw the infantry contingent.
*   Lords Langdale and Musgrave commanded Royalist English elements.

### Troop Composition

| Side | Infantry | Cavalry | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Parliamentarians | ~5,300 | ~3,700 | Figures include New Model, Lambert’s forces, and militia |
| Royalists | ~18,300 (Scottish) + ~4,500 (Royalist) | ~5,700 total | Not all were engaged; many units understrength |

A contemporary voice, likely exaggerating but telling in tone, claimed “not a fifth man could handle a pike,” a comment aimed at the poor training and morale of many Scottish troops.

* * *

Arms and Armour
---------------

Infantry were organised into regiments of musketeers and pikemen. Musketeers used four-foot, matchlock muskets, with some flintlock variants, while pikemen wielded 15–18-foot pikes, often bearing body armour and helmets.

Cavalry on both sides wore pot helmets, thigh-length boots and cuirasses or leather jerkins. Parliamentarian horsemen typically carried two pistols and a sword, their flintlocks offering better reliability in rain. Scots often bore lances instead of pistols, useful in open warfare but clumsy in Preston’s broken terrain.

Dragoons had become specialised mounted troops by 1648, some using carbines, while the Scots still clung to older matchlock muskets.

At the Battle of Preston in August 1648, the types of swords in use reflected the mixed composition of the armies and the transitional nature of mid-17th-century warfare. While firearms, pikes, and polearms dominated the battlefield, swords were still an essential sidearm for officers, cavalry, and some infantry.

**Parliamentarian New Model Army and Northern Association forces**

*   **[Mortuary swords](https://sevenswords.uk/the-mortuary-sword/)**: A distinctly English cavalry weapon, with a broad, double-edged blade, basket hilt, and decorative pommel often bearing a portrait mask. Common among Parliamentarian officers and troopers.
*   **Baskethilt broadswords**: These were increasingly common for both horse and foot soldiers, offering hand protection in close combat.
*   **[Rapiers](https://sevenswords.uk/rapier/)**: Mostly carried by officers and gentlemen; long, slender, and more suited to duelling or command presence than mass battle.
*   **[Hangers](https://sevenswords.uk/hanger-sword/)**: Short, curved blades often worn by dragoons or militia for camp defence and as a secondary weapon.

**Royalist Scottish Engager and English Royalist forces**

*   **[Scottish baskethilt broadswords](https://sevenswords.uk/scottish-basket-hilt-broadsword/)**: Sometimes called “claymores” in this period (the single-handed type, not the later two-handed highland sword). These were robust, double-edged, and ideal for hacking in close quarters.
*   **Mortuary swords**: Carried by many English Royalist cavalrymen, similar to those of the Parliamentarians.
*   **Rapiers**: Present among officers, especially in the English Royalist contingents.
*   **[Dirks](https://sevenswords.uk/scottish-dirk-the-highland-warrior-blade/) and daggers**: Secondary blades often carried by Scots alongside their broadswords.

Although pikes and muskets were the primary arms of infantry, when formations collapsed—such as in the close fighting at Ribbleton Moor and Winwick—these swords became decisive in the hand-to-hand engagements.

* * *

Archaeology
-----------

No major modern excavations of the battlefield are recorded in mainstream sources, so physical evidence remains largely in local museums, such as the Warrington Museum, which houses artefacts like musket balls and possibly frame-gun shot dating from the conflict. These finds hint at the intense close-quarters fighting, especially around Walton and Winwick.

* * *

Battle Timeline
---------------

![Image 1](https://sevenswords.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/battle-map-Preston.jpg)

**17 August**  
Cromwell surprised Hamilton’s scattered forces around Ribbleton Moor. Langdale’s infantry formed a defensive line that held off Parliamentarian cavalry with pikemen. After fierce combat, what Cromwell termed “a very stiff and sturdy resistance,” Parliamentarian infantry and local militia cracked the line and swept toward the Ribble bridge, forcing a breakthrough.

**Evening of 17 August**  
Thousands of Scots were captured as fields became littered with prisoners. Royalists regrouped south of the river as Parliamentarians secured the bridge and surrounding approaches. Cromwell declared the enemy “broken” in a letter.

**18 August**  
The Scots escaped south in the night, abandoning artillery, baggage and ammunition. The Parliamentarians pressed on relentlessly, catching and disrupting the retreat.

**19 August (Battle of Winwick)**  
Exhausted but cornered, the Scots halted near Winwick. Fierce fighting ensued. Parliamentarian cavalry pinned Scots in place while infantry attacked from the flanks. Formations broke and many fled into the church at Winwick, where they surrendered. The Scottish cavalry slipped away but many surrendered in Warrington and Uttoxeter soon after.

* * *

Contemporary Reflections
------------------------

Cromwell estimated “2,000 Royalists were killed and 9,000 captured,” though historians suggest such figures are inflated. Modern estimates put Royalist deaths around 1,000 at Preston, with 4,000 prisoners; the broader campaign, including Winwick, added about 1,000 killed and 7,000–8,000 taken prisoner.

One Scots officer, overwhelmed, “beseeched any that would to shoot him through the head,” a vivid testament to the despair of the defeated leadership.

* * *

Aftermath and Perspective
-------------------------

The battle effectively ended organised Scottish military support for the Royalists in this war. Hundreds of prisoners were sold or pressed into service overseas. Hamilton was subsequently beheaded. The execution of Charles I followed not long after. England became a republic under the Commonwealth, while Scotland ultimately fell under Cromwell’s rule.

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://annual.wikimedia.org/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

34% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

11% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally.
